Occurrences.AttributionNote: 牧牛圖頌: the unnamed lay preface author says ox-herding began in scripture and was displayed by generations of patriarchs.

Senses.Explanation: Herding an ox is an action and image, while Oxherding sequences are named picture-or-verse sets and remain a different object. The farm action of tending or herding an ox. In Chan records this action is repeatedly deployed as a comparison. When Mazu Daoyi asks Shigong Huizang what he is doing, Shigong answers that he is herding the ox; he says that whenever it enters the grass he seizes its nose and pulls it back (一回入草去，驀鼻拽將回), and Mazu replies that he truly knows how to herd it (子真牧牛). Baizhang Huaihai compares his handling of an addressee to an oxherd who holds a staff and prevents the animal from trespassing on crops (如牧牛人執杖視之，不令犯他苗稼). Yunqi Zhuhong's preface traces the expression to the comparison of watching an ox with a staff (譬如牧牛，執杖視之，不令縱逸，犯人苗稼), while Guting Shanjian explicitly says that its illustrated use compares the ox with the wild restlessness of human nature (夫謂牧牛者，譬人性之狂掉也). Yunyan Tianyou also attacks the inherited image: after the nose-rope breaks, his verse asks what excrement or wind remains to herd (牧甚屎屁). Zen bends the ordinary action into a publicly tested comparison, while the last witness shows that masters could also overturn it.

Senses.Note: Picture-and-verse and verse-only forms are variants of the same kind of titled sequence, not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: This separate sense names an Oxherding picture-or-verse sequence, not herd an ox. As a title or section label, Oxherding denotes an illustrated or versified sequence rather than the action of tending an ox. The corpus preserves Puming's Ten Oxherding Verses (普明牧牛十頌), beginning with the stage Not Yet Herded (未牧), and Zhufeng Xu's record separately heads a sequence Oxherding Verses (牧牛頌). A named textual or pictorial sequence is a different thing from the action it depicts, so this use receives its own sense.
